title: Interposer that is itself a capacity-tier DRAM
idea: Po: the interposer is the memory. Fabricate the ~2,500 mm2 2.5D silicon interposer, today passive wiring, on a mature trench-capacitor DRAM node so the silicon under and between GPU and HBM becomes a slower but very near capacity tier of several GB, wired to the GPU through the interposer's own dense metal.
why: Turns wasted interposer silicon into bits at mature-node cost per bit with no TSV tax; adds ~4-16 GB per package at <1 pJ/bit with no new EUV capital.

title: Pinless DRAM die fed data by light through its backside
idea: Po: memory with no pins. A VCSEL array in the package lid shines modulated light onto Ge photodiode and micro-LED tiles on each thinned DRAM die's backside, so the bumps carry only power and ground and each die exchanges data with the logic die through free space.
why: Removes signal TSVs and microbumps (HBM TSV tax) and decouples die count from bump field; targets ~0.5 pJ/bit and 2x more dies per package footprint.

title: Wireless in-package multicast of shared weights to many GPUs
idea: Po: memory that shouts instead of whispers. One weights-holding DRAM stack drives a 140 GHz antenna into the metal package lid cavity, which acts as a shared waveguide, so all eight accelerators in the package receive the same weight stream at once instead of each storing its own copy.
why: Model weights are replicated per GPU; de-duplication frees 30-60% of HBM capacity for KV cache, and one transmission serving N readers cuts energy per reader-bit ~N-fold.

title: Mirrored predictors so only residuals cross the memory bus
idea: Po: memory sends guesses, not data. The HBM base die and the GPU memory controller run identical tiny value predictors (last-value, stride and delta per cacheline region) in lockstep; on each read only the entropy-coded residual against the shared prediction crosses the link.
why: Attacks 3-4 pJ/bit data-movement energy; structured tensors and pointers compress 1.5-3x, raising effective bandwidth and cutting link energy by the same factor.

title: Bit-plane-major tensor layout with on-demand mantissa streaming
idea: Po: throw data away before it moves. Store tensors bit-plane-major so the interface ships sign, exponent and top mantissa planes first; the accelerator requests lower planes only for tiles whose running error estimate exceeds a threshold, so most low bits never leave the DRAM.
why: 2-3x effective bandwidth and interface energy for inference, and less row overfetch per useful bit.

title: Shingled staircase HBM wired by printed edge traces
idea: Po: holes in silicon are forbidden. Offset each DRAM die ~200 um like a NAND staircase and connect the exposed edge pads with aerosol-jet-printed copper traces running down the steps to the base die, giving a TSV-free stack with a few thousand edge links.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss), letting core dies cost like DDR5 dies while keeping a wide stacked interface.

title: Origami stack: one thinned die folded into eight layers
idea: Po: chips are folded, not stacked. Fabricate eight DRAM arrays on one reticle-stitched strip, thin it to ~15 um with polyimide-backed hinge zones carrying continuous metal, and fold it accordion-style so every inter-layer link is an ordinary on-die wire running through a fold.
why: No TSVs and no bonding steps, so stack yield loss from TSV/bond defects disappears; thousands of fold wires at 2 um pitch give HBM-class width.

title: Frequency-multiplexed RF carriers sharing each TSV
idea: Po: one wire, many voices. Each TSV carries four RF carriers (5-20 GHz) from tiny on-die oscillators and mixers, and each die listens through its own band-pass filter, so one TSV does the work of four and bandwidth can be reassigned between dies on the fly.
why: Cuts signal TSV count ~4x and recovers keep-out-zone area, shrinking the HBM TSV area tax.

title: Acoustic bus: GHz sound waves through stacked silicon
idea: Po: memory talks by sound. Thin-film AlScN transducers on every die launch and detect 3-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses that propagate vertically through the bonded silicon stack, carrying command, address and refresh-sync broadcasts with no TSV at all.
why: Frees all command/address TSVs for data and broadcasts to every die in one shot; trims TSV count and periphery.

title: Voltage-stacked HBM recycling one current through every die
idea: Po: every die stands on a different ground. Wire the 8-16 dies' supplies in series (die k between kV and (k+1)V), feed the stack at ~12 V, and use small on-die switched-capacitor balancers plus level-shifted signalling so the same current flows through all dies.
why: Supply current and power TSV/bump count drop 8-16x; since power and ground are a large share of TSVs, stack area and PDN loss fall sharply.

title: Free-space optical memory links through immersion coolant
idea: Po: the liquid is the wire. In immersion-cooled racks, memory sleds and accelerator boards face each other through the dielectric fluid and exchange data over arrays of collimated micro-LED and photodiode pixels (imaging links), replacing copper backplanes and cables.
why: Makes rack-scale disaggregated memory cheap (~1 pJ/bit, no connectors), recovering the 20-30% of DRAM stranded in fixed servers.

title: Laser-written waveguides inside glass interposers link HBM optically
idea: Po: wires are written, not printed. Femtosecond lasers write buried 3D waveguides inside a glass interposer that connect edge-coupled micro-ring transmitters on the HBM base die to the GPU, routing hundreds of WDM channels in 3D with zero lithography.
why: Lets HBM sit 5-50 mm away, breaking the GPU shoreline limit (more stacks per GPU) at ~1 pJ/bit and with no interposer masks.

title: Wavelength-addressed rack memory pool with passive grating routers
idea: Po: an address is a colour. Each pooled DRAM module owns a laser wavelength, and a passive arrayed-waveguide grating router connects any accelerator to any module just by tuning its transmitter, so no electronic switch sits in the memory path.
why: Pooling raises usable memory supply 20-40% with no new fabs, at switchless latency and low pJ/bit.

title: Harvest HBM stacks from retired accelerators onto new boards
idea: Po: dead GPUs are memory mines. Run a laser-assisted debond and reball line that lifts HBM stacks off retired or failed accelerator interposers, re-tests them, and mounts them on a low-cost organic carrier as CXL or inference memory modules.
why: DRAM outlives the 3-4 year accelerator cycle; recycling adds supply with no wafer starts, cutting scarce-resource and capital use per bit.

title: Self-healing interposer with GeTe switches rerouting dead bumps
idea: Po: the package rewires itself after it is built. Embed phase-change GeTe RF switches in the interposer routing layer so that, after assembly test, channels are re-routed around open microbumps or bad TSV lanes by pulsing the switches once.
why: HBM assembly yield is down 20-30% and one bad stack can scrap a whole module; post-assembly repair recovers most of that loss.

title: Reel-to-reel DRAM tape wrapped around a cooling pipe
idea: Po: memory is sold by the metre. Mount bare DRAM dies on a continuous copper-on-polyimide tape (tape-automated bonding style) with fine-line flex wiring, then wrap the tape helically around a liquid-cooled tube to form a cylindrical module plugged in at one end.
why: Low-capex reel-to-reel assembly that U.S. flex-circuit makers can run, with no interposer and excellent cooling.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive links inside the HBM stack
idea: Po: time is abolished. Replace the stack's source-synchronous DDR interface with 1-of-4 delay-insensitive asynchronous encoding on TSVs and microbumps, deleting DLLs, PLLs and link training so lanes idle at zero power and run as fast as voltage and temperature allow.
why: Shrinks PHY periphery and idle power and enables deep voltage scaling; ~30% interface energy cut.

title: Room-temperature nanowire-velcro bonding for DRAM stacks
idea: Po: joints are grown, not soldered. Electrodeposit dense Cu nanowire forests on both bond faces; pressing them together interlocks the wires into a conductive mechanical joint at room temperature, avoiding reflow or 300-400 C anneals.
why: Protects DRAM retention (leakage tail) from thermal budget and allows ~3 um pitch and rework, cutting stack yield loss.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods with superconducting YBCO interposer wiring
idea: Po: wires have no resistance. Run memory pods at 77 K and pattern YBCO superconducting lines on the interposer, so links from many DRAM stacks to the processor are lossless over 10-100 mm, while cold DRAM retains data ~1000x longer.
why: Lossless long interposer wires allow low-swing signalling and more stacks per GPU, and cold retention nearly removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Resonant charge-recovery drivers that recycle bus wire energy
idea: Po: wires give their energy back. Drive memory data lines through small on-die inductors so each line resonates; line capacitance swings adiabatically and most of the CV2 charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Breaks the CV2 voltage floor on interface wires; 2-4x lower link energy per bit at the same swing.

title: Books-on-a-shelf: DRAM dies standing edge-on over logic
idea: Po: the stack lies on its side. Stand thinned DRAM dies upright like books, each bonded along one polished edge carrying fine-pitch pads to the logic die beneath, with coolant flowing in the gaps between dies.
why: No TSVs and no stack height limit; every die is cooled directly and wired straight to logic, raising capacity per package without the TSV tax.

title: Descriptor-driven HBM: send access programs, not addresses
idea: Po: the processor never names an address. The GPU sends compact tensor access descriptors (base, strides, tile shape) to an address generator on the HBM base die, which walks rows in bank-friendly order and streams data back without per-line commands.
why: Frees command/address pins and link energy, and lets the stack fetch full rows usefully, cutting overfetch energy per useful bit.

title: Cloud billing per byte crossing the HBM interface
idea: Po: moving data costs money, storing it is free. Cloud providers meter and price bytes crossing each accelerator's memory interface and refund locality-friendly jobs, steering frameworks toward fusion and on-chip reuse so fleets need fewer HBM stacks.
why: Software-driven traffic cuts of 20-40% let the same DRAM supply serve more workloads; a market fix for a supply squeeze.

title: Inductive coil links replace TSVs with one top-metal mask
idea: Po: dies talk by magnetism. One added thick top-metal mask forms coil arrays on each DRAM die; dies are stacked face-to-back with no TSVs, data crosses by near-field inductive coupling through the thinned silicon, and power arrives by edge wire bonds.
why: Removes TSV etch, liner, fill and reveal steps (HBM TSV tax) for a single mask; ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vertical links.

title: Capacitive kiss pads for removable DRAM-on-logic stacking
idea: Po: memory and logic touch without bonding. A single added mask patterns thin-passivated capacitive plates on the DRAM top metal; the die is pressed face-to-face onto matching logic plates with no metal bond, so signals cross by capacitive coupling and the die can be removed.
why: Gives HBM-class density with zero bonding yield loss and full rework; KGD problem disappears.

title: Optical backscatter pixels: DRAM reflects instead of emitting light
idea: Po: memory that reflects rather than shines. One mask etches micro-cavities in the top dielectric over an existing metal layer used as a mirror; a blanket electro-optic polymer fills them, and the top electrode modulates how much of the lid laser's light each pixel reflects to a detector array.
why: Optical I/O with no laser or photodetector on the DRAM die and one mask; potential ~0.3 pJ/bit and thousands of parallel lanes.

title: Millimetre-wave backscatter antennas on each DRAM die
idea: Po: the memory answers without speaking. One top-metal mask adds a small antenna per die; the GPU floods the package cavity with a 140 GHz carrier and each die returns read data by switching its antenna load with a single transistor, RFID-style.
why: Near-zero transmit power on the DRAM die and no TSV or bump for read return; strong energy per bit gain for wide broadcast-style reads.

title: Expose commodity DDR5 internal wide bus through one pad mask
idea: Po: the inside of the chip becomes the outside. On a standard DDR5 die, one added pad mask brings the wide internal global I/O lines up to hybrid-bond pads so a logic die bonded face-to-face reads them directly, skipping the DDR serializer and PHY.
why: Turns high-volume DDR wafers into HBM-like wide memory without TSVs or a new die design; ~3-5x lower pJ/bit than DDR5 I/O.

title: Single-metal-layer bridge enabled by mirrored crossing-free ballouts
idea: Po: an interposer with only one wiring layer. Co-design HBM and GPU bump maps as mirror images so every connection routes without crossings, then build the bridge die with just one patterned 1 um copper layer in a mature fab.
why: Cuts bridge or interposer masks from 4-6 to one, slashing 2.5D cost and letting U.S. mature fabs make the parts.

title: Undiced DRAM tiles stitched across scribe lanes by one mask
idea: Po: the wafer is never diced. Leave 4x4 groups of DRAM dies attached; one added top-metal mask stitches a wide shared bus across the scribe lanes to a central bond field where a processor chiplet is bonded face-to-face.
why: Removes interposer, microbumps and per-die packaging for a 16-die memory tile; capacity per package rises 4x at low pJ/bit.

title: Power fed from the lid into the top of HBM stacks
idea: Po: power falls from the sky. One backside mask adds power landing pads on the top die of each stack; a copper lid with compliant pins injects current into the top of the existing power TSV columns, so power enters from both ends.
why: Halves stack IR drop and frees about half of the bottom power bumps for extra signal channels, raising bandwidth per stack ~1.3-1.5x.

title: Liquid-metal microwell interconnects that never freeze
idea: Po: the solder stays liquid forever. One mask patterns microwells in a polymer layer, a gallium alloy fills them by squeegee, and the mating die's pads dip into the wells, giving fine-pitch joints that absorb thermal mismatch and can be reworked.
why: Removes solder-fatigue and warpage yield loss in large HBM packages and allows reuse of stacks; no reflow heat on DRAM.

title: Stress-metal microsprings for socketed, re-testable HBM
idea: Po: the bumps are springs. A single mask patterns stress-graded MoCr fingers on the DRAM pad field; a release etch lets them curl up into microsprings that press-contact the interposer, so stacks can be tested at speed and swapped before final lock-down.
why: Fixes the known-good-stack problem: bad stacks are caught and replaced instead of scrapping a whole package; 10-20% package yield gain.

title: Universal pre-built interposer customised by a single via mask
idea: Po: every package uses the same package. Pre-fabricate a standard interposer with a dense crossbar of horizontal and vertical lines in volume, and personalise each product with only one via mask that connects chosen crossings.
why: Amortises interposer masks across all products; per-product mask cost and lead time drop ~5x, lowering capital per memory package.

title: Interposers made from reclaimed monitor and reject wafers
idea: Po: fab garbage is the interposer. Collect test, monitor and scratched prime wafers, re-polish them, laser-drill vias with no mask, and add one thick copper redistribution layer with a single mask for simple HBM-to-logic routing.
why: Removes demand for new silicon and crucible-grown wafers in interposers, cutting cost and quartz-crucible exposure.

title: Self-assembling copolymer wires quadruple interposer wiring density
idea: Po: wires draw themselves. One coarse guide mask sets trenches on the interposer, and a block-copolymer film self-assembles inside them into 4x finer lines that become copper wires after pattern transfer and plating.
why: 4x more die-to-die wires per mm of shoreline without EUV or extra masks, raising HBM channel count per GPU edge.

title: Magnetically chained conductive film replaces microbumps
idea: Po: the glue is the wire. Only one pad-opening mask is used; an adhesive film loaded with nickel particles is cured in a vertical magnetic field so the particles line up into columns that conduct only along z at ~5 um pitch.
why: Removes bump plating, reflow and underfill steps, lowering assembly cost and thermal stress on DRAM.

title: Capillary self-assembly places hundreds of DRAM dies at once
idea: Po: chips swim to their sockets. One mask defines hydrophilic bond sites on the target wafer; water droplets pull hundreds of DRAM dies into sub-micron alignment in parallel before hybrid bonding.
why: Die-to-wafer bonding throughput up ~10x versus pick-and-place, cutting stacking cost and tool count.

title: Light elevator: optical broadcast through windows in stacked dies
idea: Po: the chip is a window. One mask both opens a metal-free optical shaft through each die's wiring and defines a silicon ion implant forming a defect-mediated 1550 nm detector that absorbs a few percent, so one beam from the base die broadcasts clock and commands to all 16 dies in turn.
why: Deletes clock and command/address TSVs for a single mask and gives jitter-free broadcast to every die.

title: Laser-drilled TSVs with a single backside landing mask
idea: Po: holes are drilled by light, not printed. Ultrafast lasers drill TSVs maskless through thinned DRAM after front-end and wiring are done, and the only added mask patterns the backside landing pads.
why: Removes the TSV litho, deep etch and their masks from the DRAM flow, easing the HBM TSV tax with lower capital.

title: Dual-ported HBM stack serving two GPU chiplets
idea: Po: the memory has two front doors. One added redistribution mask on the base die creates a second bump field on the opposite edge, so one stack sits between two GPU chiplets and both read the same data without copies.
why: Shared weights and KV cache need no duplicate copy; effective capacity per GPU pair up 30-50%.

title: PCB-shop panel packaging with one stepper mask for die field
idea: Po: the memory package is made in a print shop. Large panels are patterned by maskless laser direct imaging for all coarse layers, and only the fine-pitch die-attach field uses one stepper mask, so U.S. PCB fabs can build HBM-class packages.
why: Onshore packaging capacity at lower capital per unit, easing the U.S. manufacturability gap.

title: Air-gap interposer wires halve memory link capacitance
idea: Po: the best insulator is nothing. One mask defines where a sacrificial fill between interposer lines is later removed, leaving air gaps around long HBM-to-GPU wires.
why: Wire capacitance falls 2-3x, so CV2 energy on interposer links drops the same amount; ~1.5 pJ/bit saved on 3-4 pJ/bit HBM links.

title: Thick-copper superhighway layer for low-swing bank-to-PHY transport
idea: Po: wires thicker than transistors are tall. One added mask lays a 10-20 um thick copper top layer that carries global data from far banks to the I/O with very low resistance, so data can move at 100-200 mV swing.
why: Cuts on-die data movement energy (a large part of the 5.9 pJ per useful bit) ~2x without new transistors.

title: Face-to-face DRAM pairs halve TSVs in HBM stacks
idea: Po: dies kiss in pairs. One hybrid-bond pad mask lets two DRAM dies bond face-to-face, so each pair needs TSVs in only one die and an 8-high stack needs TSV processing on 4 dies.
why: Half as much TSV processing and keep-out area, easing the HBM TSV area and yield tax.

title: Sacrificial shorting bar removes ESD circuits from bonded links
idea: Po: memory with no protection. One top-metal mask adds a shorting bar that grounds every die-to-die pad during handling and bonding, then is laser-cut after assembly, so the I/O needs no ESD diodes.
why: ESD structures add area and pad capacitance; removing them cuts PHY area and per-bit link energy 20-40%.
